newsitem.title: MEXICO: Top Latam writers went from limericks to literature.
newsitem.headline: Top Latam writers went from limericks to literature.

text.p: Two of Latin America's top novelists started writing by composing bawdy verse when they were at school together to counter the rigours of a strict British education, one of them has disclosed.

With disciplinarian teachers as common enemies, Mexican novelist Carlos Fuentes and fellow prize-winning writer Jose Donoso of Chile were naughty scribblers long before they became masters of literature.

"We used to get our own back by making up limericks about those teachers we particularly disliked," Fuentes said on Sunday at the launching of a posthumous novel whose manuscript Donoso completed shortly before he died of cancer in December.
Limericks are five-line rhyming verses that are heavily ironic and often verge on the obscene. The ones he recited were so lewd they were unquotable.

"We had to do gymnastics in the freezing cold at 7 a.m. and then eat porridge like something out of Oliver Twist," Fuentes said of his education in the 1940s at The Grange, a British school in Santiago.

Fuentes, whose father was a diplomat in Chile, said he and Donoso were often "caned", the traditional but now outlawed British practice of corporal punishment involving the striking of wayward pupils with a bamboo cane.
But their literary wit was not beaten out of them.
Fuentes said Donoso despaired of school and ran away at 16 to work as a sheep-shearer, but later found his vocation and became Chile's most reknowned novelist.

Along with Colombia's Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Donoso and Fuentes became part of a "boom" generation of Latin American novelists in the 1960's, when the region stopped being a literary backwater and its books won worldwide readership and critical acclaim.
